lessons.title: एक, दोन, तीन, चार, पाच — one to five
lessons.gloss: one to five — nearly Hindi's, with two tells in the spelling and one in the sound

segments.text: Marathi and Hindi both use Devanagari and both descend from Sanskrit, so their numbers look almost identical. Almost is where the interest is.

blocks.title: You'll want to know: the five

utterances: 4. Marathi: चार. said: chār — but see below.

blocks.title: What you've built: three Marathi tells

segments.text: Set them against Hindi. Two differences are visible and one is audible:

utterances: number: 2. Hindi: दो do. Marathi: दोन don: final n.
number: 5. Hindi: पाँच pāṁch. Marathi: पाच pāch: no nasal mark.
number: 4. Hindi: चार chār. Marathi: चार tsār: same spelling, different sound.

segments.text: Do not explain all three histories yet. First make the five forms automatic; the next lesson earns the deeper comparison.

segments.instruction: the visible tells — don has n; pāch has no nasal mark
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the visible tells — *don* has *n*; *pāch* has no nasal mark]

segments.instruction: the audible tell — written chār, Marathi tsār
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the audible tell — written *chār*, Marathi *tsār*]

segments.text: Count to five in Marathi. (Ek, don, tīn, tsār, pāch.) Where does Marathi add a letter compared with Hindi? (दोन, don.) Which form drops a nasal mark? (पाच, pāch.) What differs in चार without differing in spelling? (Marathi's च is nearer ts before ā.) Next: explain where those differences came from.

lessons.title: Why Marathi two rhymes with three
lessons.gloss: why Marathi two rhymes with three, and why Hindi preserves a different piece of five

segments.text: Count once: ek, don, tīn, tsār, pāch. Which two words end in n? (Don and tīn.)

blocks.title: The word, taken apart — दोन borrowed from “three”

segments.text: The tempting guess is that Marathi दोन don kept something Hindi दो do lost. It did not.
Sanskrit's neuter word for three, त्रीणि trī́ṇi, became Prakrit tiṇṇi. In three, the ṇ genuinely belongs to the word. The doubled consonant is a Prakrit trade for the lost r.

The word for two was then reshaped to match its neighbour: Prakrit doṇṇi copied the shape of tiṇṇi. Marathi don's final n is therefore an innovation, a rhyme borrowed from the number next door. Hindi do simply never took it.
English numbers did this too: four acquired its initial f- by analogy with five. Familiar sequences pull neighbouring words toward one another.

blocks.title: What you've built: पाच and the nasal Hindi kept

segments.text: Marathi पाच pāch and Hindi पाँच pāṁch tell the opposite story. Hindi's chandrabindu ँ records the nasal of Sanskrit pañca; Marathi's spelling drops it.
So neither language is simply “older.” Marathi innovated in don, while Hindi retained an older feature in pāṁch. Comparing both descendants reveals the history that either one alone could hide.

blocks.title: Sounds you'll need: चार and the change its spelling hides

segments.text: Both write चार, but Marathi pronounces च before ā nearer ts: tsār. The letters stayed aligned while the sound moved.

segments.instruction: same spelling, shifted sound — chār / tsār
segments.source: [YOU SAY: same spelling, shifted sound — *chār / tsār*]

segments.text: Did Marathi don preserve an ancient ending? (No: two copied three.) Which language retains Sanskrit pañca's nasal in writing? (Hindi.) Why can neither daughter be called simply older? (Each changed or retained a different feature.) What does Marathi change without respelling चार? (Ch shifts toward ts before ā.)

segments.prompt: Did Marathi don preserve an ancient final n?
acceptedResponses: it copied the pattern of three

feedback.correct: Correct: don's final n arose by analogy with the word for three.
feedback.incorrect: No. Marathi two copied the pattern of three; the final n is not an ancient ending.
